messages.subject: About using model test to evaluate different landscape evolution scenarios
messages.subject_clean: About using model test to evaluate different landscape evolution scenarios
messages.body_plain:
Hi there. I hope you are all doing well.

I'm here to ask an important question regarding the AIC in BioGeoBEARS. One of the most interesting things about BioGeoBEARS is the possibility to use the Time Stratified Matrix to identify the landscape evolution. And, despite it being an arbitrary setup, we can use it to our advantage to seek the best reconstruction model and the best scenario. My question is: what are your thoughts about using different matrices to test different landscape evolution scenarios using AIC?

Let me give an example. Imagine that there is a scenario in the literature that concludes that the emergence of a landmass occurred around 2 million years. However, another scenario also exists that says that the same landmass occurred much earlier, around 10 million years. Would it be wise to use two distinct models, let's say, DEC with a matrix with scenario A and the same DEC with a matrix with scenario B, to test these scenarios using AIC? I'm mean, even if AIC tells me that one or another DEC is better, would it be wise to consider that, in fact, this scenario is the best to explain my data?

Thanks for your insights.

Cheers,

messages.body_plain:
Hi, great questions!  We have some more discussion of this issue in Klaus & Matzke (2020, Sys Bio), where we had to deal with the possibility that New Zealand and/or New Calendonia were totally submerged at some point.  So we compared some models, although you will see from the Discussion section of that paper that we had a lot of reasons to be skeptical of how it worked in that case.  Quick answers:

On Friday, May 7, 2021 at 6:50:47 AM UTC+12 mpnogu...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi there. I hope you are all doing well.
>
> I'm here to ask an important question regarding the AIC in BioGeoBEARS. One of the most interesting things about BioGeoBEARS is the possibility to use the Time Stratified Matrix to identify the landscape evolution. And, despite it being an arbitrary setup, we can use it to our advantage to seek the best reconstruction model and the best scenario. My question is: what are your thoughts about using different matrices to test different landscape evolution scenarios using AIC?
>
> Let me give an example. Imagine that there is a scenario in the literature that concludes that the emergence of a landmass occurred around 2 million years. However, another scenario also exists that says that the same landmass occurred much earlier, around 10 million years. Would it be wise to use two distinct models, let's say, DEC with a matrix with scenario A and the same DEC with a matrix with scenario B, to test these scenarios using AIC?

Yes, this is basically a valid approach. However, some thoughts:

* You would want to make some effort to also account for other likely improvements in model fit -- e.g., compare DEC vs DEC+J, DIVALIKE, etc., and also at least use the "+x" model addition to include distance-dependent dispersal, since this is almost-always an important improvement.

* You would take your suite of base models and run them under the 2 paleogeography scenarios

> I'm mean, even if AIC tells me that one or another DEC is better, would it be wise to consider that, in fact, this scenario is the best to explain my data?

It would just be a statement of fact that whatever model is the best fit, is the best fit.  BUT this statement only applies AMONG the models you have run.  There could always be a better-fit model which you haven't run, because you didn't think of it or (most likely) no one in the world has thought of it/programmed it.   Reality is always far more complex than our models, our models are just rough approximations.

Other caveats:
* BioGeoBEARS/Lagrange-style models ignore lineage extinction, this is probably particularly important e.g. in cases where landmasses are sinking/coming up. It would be better to use extinction-aware models, but these get very slow for typically large biogeography problems. (But google GeoSSE or GeoHiSSE for what exists.)
* All of the above assumes that the dating of your phylogeny is correct and matches one of the paleogeographic scenarios.  Obviously there could be a lot of issues there.

Cheers!
Nick

messages.subject: Time-stratified dispersal counts
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nick,

I am running time-stratified analyses with the aim to retrieve dispersal counts using stochastic mapping. These analyses run smoothly, but the output file "all_dispersals_counts_fromto_means.txt" is just the sum across all time bins. Is there a way to get the dispersal counts separately for each of the different time bins?
Many thanks in advance,
Ben

messages.subject: Script for running stochastic maps over a sample of trees
messages.subject_clean: Script for running stochastic maps over a sample of trees
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

For a while my research group has been interested in running biogeographic stochastic maps over a sample of trees to account for phylogenetic uncertainty when counting events and estimating the timing of dispersal events. We have finally wrapped up a script that does that, and summarizes the results in a friendly way. It can be found here: https://github.com/ivanlfm/BGB_BSM_multiple_trees

During the elaboration of the script, we found that it is especially useful to include phylogenetic uncertainty when:

(1) one wants to estimate the timing of dispersals using a +J model. This is because in +J models, dispersal is associated to node ages, and using a single tree will mean that the estimate is strongly biased to the age of the node in that particular tree.

(2) one is testing a biogeographic hypothesis and the age estimates cross the boundaries of time slices (as Nick had suggested in an earlier post).

We demonstrate this with a nice example of the colonization of the Galapagos by a group of spiders. If you are interested, you can read the manuscript, which I just posted as a pre-print. It has just been submitted to a journal, so any feedback/comments/suggestions/critiques are mostly welcome:

https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.05.11.443682v1

Thanks!
Best,
Ivan

messages.subject: No parallelisation in time-stratified analyses?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have noticed that speed-up of analyses using parallelization doesn't seem to work for time-stratified analyses. Can anybody confirm that?

I am currently running the different possible perturbations of +d, +w, and time stratification on a big linux cluster. All non-stratified analyses make full use of the cores allocated (up to 64), whereas in the time-stratified analyses at least 90% of the cores are constantly idle.

Maybe time-stratification somehow prevents parallelization, or it hasn't been implemented yet for parallelization?

Cheers,
Ben

messages.body_plain:
Dear friends,

I would like a help, because I'm a little inexperienced in R.

I've been running the BioGeoBEARS script. Even with all packages and version of R (4.1.0) updated, according to comments here in the group. When I enter the function:

runslow = TRUE
resfn = "Psychotria_DEC_M0_unconstrained_v1.Rdata"
if (runslow)
    {
    res = bears_optim_run (BioGeoBEARS_run_object)
    res

    save (res, file = resfn)
    resDEC = res
    } else {
    # Loads to "res"
    load (resfn)
    resDEC = res
    }

I get the error message:
Error in assign ("last.warning", NULL, envir = baseenv ()):
  it is not possible to add 'last.warning' binding to the base environment

I don't really know where the error is, as all the previous functions to it don't give me error message.

Before BioGeoBEARS ran well, but when I migrated to the new R, I believe there was an error in the installation or conflict with previous versions of the packages (even uninstalled and checked to uninstall them).

>From now on, I thank you immensely!
Lamarck
